correctionToRoundSeven: Round 7's handoff said 'recovery mechanism unidentified'. It is identified: at the pre-fix tree the room was rescued by its own settlement meeting the durable gate — three `dispatch: settle document` refusals two seconds apart (the settle default, docs/service.go:517), maxSettleFailures of them (service.go:36), the third calling failRoomLocked (retrySettleLocked, service.go:995), closing the room at 6.0 s. The three log lines were read from a run at the pre-fix tree (555a7e36) at 23:20:11.876, 23:20:13.881 and 23:20:15.886 for one room, each carrying `the document's room is behind its durable head`. The refusal doing the recovering is ErrRoomBehindHead, which this pull request adds, so that recovery is one half of this change rescuing the other half and not a safety net that predates the finding.

proof.criterion: The deferred re-examination closes a room the eviction interval refused, in the branch where a settlement could also have rescued it: the severity's first branch, stated in seconds.
proof.surface: Two real envoy-dispatch processes on one Postgres 17 and one nats-server 2.10 in this issue's pod, with a document websocket holding the room on A and the burst made through B's HTTP API; the trailing write lands inside the two-second eviction interval the first write started, so its notification is one the interval refuses, and nothing writes the document again.
proof.observed: The room closed 1.947 s, 1.944 s and 1.946 s after the trailing write across three runs — the window's own length. The row asserts the document owes a settlement at that moment, so it is the branch it is named for.
proof.negativeControl: Driven on a scratch clone of this head with NextWake/OnWake unwired from the listener and the reconnect sweep left in place: the room closed 6.018 s after the trailing write instead, which is the settlement path — three gate refusals ending in failRoomLocked — taking over. So for this branch the wake is an improvement in latency from 6.0 s to 1.9 s, and not the only path.

proof.criterion: The deferred re-examination closes a room no settlement of this process will fail: the branch the wake was built for, where nothing else closes the room at all. This is the severity's second branch, and the one that decides whether the fix is load-bearing.
proof.surface: The same two processes and the same burst, with A started under a settle delay no window of the row reaches (DISPATCH_TEST_SETTLE_DELAY=30m, under the test hooks) and the document created and written on B, so no settlement of A's can fire and the window's re-examination is the only path left.
proof.observed: The room closed 1.876 s, 1.948 s and 1.945 s after the trailing write across three runs, and no `dispatch: settle document` line for that room appeared in A's output, so nothing but the window could have closed it.
proof.negativeControl: The same scratch clone with the wake unwired: the reader kept the room, with no second eviction in 30 s and none in 45 s on the earlier run of the same shape. Per the reviewer's discriminator (Envoy b3fe1be11b4f3380806f329e4a71b80a), the evictor's own lines were silent there — no failed-Evict line and neither head-read line — so the wake never reached the room, which is the unwired behaviour rather than a re-examination that reached no verdict. So for this branch the fix is load-bearing: wake wired, about 1.9 s; wake unwired, never.

proof.criterion: The construction of that room is deliberate, and the record says what it is and is not.
proof.surface: The two rows' own code and comments, and the run that rejected the first construction.
proof.command: cd packages/envoy && . /legion/harness/env.sh && go test -tags multiprocess -count=1 -run TestTheRefusedNotificationCloses ./cmd/dispatch   (the first construction, before it was replaced)
proof.observed: Measured: A cannot settle, so no settlement of this process will fail that room. Inferred, and written as an inference: a room that owes nothing has no settlement to fire and so reaches the same state by another road, which is why removing the rescuer is the stronger isolation — it leaves the window as the only remaining path whatever else is armed. The literal owes-nothing construction was tried first and did not hold: B was given a 100 ms settle delay so its write's pending row cleared before A's reconnect loaded the room, the row asserted that row absent at the load and it was, and the room still settled — A's own reconnecting peer appends as it syncs and arms a settlement of its own. With the wake wired that assertion passed only because the window (1.88 s) beat the settle delay (2 s), a vacuous pass; the unwired control is what exposed it, closing at 6.02 s with A's settle line present.
proof.negativeControl: That rejected construction is itself the control on the rig: a row whose condition does not hold passes for the wrong reason while the fix is in place and only its own control reveals it, which is why both rows assert the state they depend on rather than only the outcome.

writeThroughRetrying503s, in the same commit, carries the instrument lesson in its comment: a write whose own room is failed or reloading is answered 503 DOC_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE and the contract is that the client repeats the call, so a rig that treats it as a failure reports a correct contract as a defect. One run of this row's first draft did exactly that.
notes: Severity, stated in seconds for both branches as the architect asked: a room with a settlement owed is closed by the window in about 1.9 s and, without the window, by the durable gate's three refusals in about 6.0 s; a room no settlement will fail is closed by the window in about 1.9 s and, without it, not at all. The review's finding is therefore right for the second branch and overstated for the first, and the fix is load-bearing.

Raised by the reviewer for its own round and not tested here, recorded so it is not lost: once dueRooms has taken a room out of the deferred set, documentChanged can bail at the unlocked head read, at the locked confirmation or at a failed Evict, and none of those paths re-arms the window or puts the room back. My rows measure the path that reaches a verdict; the error paths are the reviewer's finding to make.

Also from the reviewer, for the census rather than for me: the sixteen-edit measurement of round 6 is a real result but cannot carry a claim that an API write is never refused with ErrRoomBehindHead — that route holds the document's advisory lock from before its fork and is structurally immune, while the applyLive callers that fork unlocked are not.

Carried and still the operator's: dispatch-multiprocess is not in the required set (lint, typecheck, test, pr-title are), so the two rows added here would not block a merge if they went red. The check-runs endpoint's default page of thirty also hides the four required lanes behind this commit's twelve pr-title rows; read it with per_page=100.
